title: MATH 107: Introduction to Linear Algebra
text:
Welcome
This website contains materials for MATH 107: Introduction to Linear Algebra (3 units, GE Area 2) at Cal Poly Humboldt. Class meets face to face Monday, Wednesday, and Friday, 10:00–10:50 a.m., in FR 201.
Catalog description: Euclidean spaces, matrices and matrix arithmetic, solving systems of equations, and eigenvalues and eigenvectors. Emphasis on applications and use of computation.
This site follows three units: representing and comparing things with vectors; transforming, solving, simulating, and computing with matrices; then explaining dynamics, fitting data, and exploiting structure (eigenvectors, least squares, SVD). Daily learning objectives are on Lectures. Class outlines for later meetings will be posted before those days.

title: MATH 107: Introduction to Linear Algebra
text:
What you’ll learn
By the end of the course you should be able to:

Interpret matrices, vectors, and complex numbers, both algebraically and geometrically.
Solve systems of linear equations using row-reduction techniques by hand and with software.
Find eigenvalues and eigenvectors of a matrix by hand for a \(2\times 2\) matrix and with software for general cases.
Understand and apply eigenvalues and eigenvectors to solve problems.
Recognize special types of matrices and their properties, such as triangular, symmetric, and positive definite matrices.
Communicate in the language of linear algebra, including linear combination, subspace, span, independence, basis, and dimension.
Write or adapt programs to implement linear algebra concepts, such as matrix arithmetic, vectors, and plotting.
Apply linear algebra to real-world problems.
Learn independently as well as collaboratively. Develop study techniques that include pre- and post-reading of class materials and be able to critically analyze and implement solutions in a team setting.

Daily objectives for each meeting are on the lectures page.

Three song feature vectors (loudness, tempo) — units already scaled for today: \[

title: Lab 1 — Finding Similar Things
text:
Application (~15 min)
C1.1. Compute \(\lVert a-b\rVert\) and \(\lVert a-c\rVert\) (Euclidean).
Expected: \(\lVert a-b\rVert=\sqrt{2}\approx 1.414\); \(\lVert a-c\rVert=\sqrt{18}=3\sqrt{2}\approx 4.243\).

Python: np.linalg.norm(a-b)

Expected: \(b\) is nearer; among these two songs, \(b\) is more similar to \(a\) in (loudness, tempo).
C1.3 (scale warning). Replace \(c\) by \(c_{\mathrm{bad}}=(4,30)\) (tempo mistyped \(\times 10\)). Recompute \(\lVert a-c_{\mathrm{bad}}\rVert\). Does the nearest neighbor of \(a\) among \(\{b,c_{\mathrm{bad}}\}\) change?
Expected: distance becomes large (\(\approx 28.16\)); NN is still \(b\), but the gap is dominated by the bad scale — feature units matter.

C6.1. Compute the SVD of \(M\). List the singular values (largest to smallest).
Expected: singular values \(8,4,4,0\) (or equivalent ordering with a zero).
C6.2. Build the rank-\(k=1\) approximation \(M_1\) and the rank-\(k=2\) approximation \(M_2\). Report \(\|M-M_k\|_F\) for each \(k\).
Expected: residual drops when \(k\) goes from \(1\) to \(2\) (exact numbers depend on rounding; \(k=2\) should be clearly smaller).
C6.3. Storage: for an \(m\times n\) matrix, truncated SVD stores about \(k(m+n+1)\) numbers. For this \(4\times4\) matrix, compute \(k(m+n+1)\) for \(k=1\) and \(k=2\). For a \(100\times 100\) grayscale image, which \(k\) values stay under half of \(100\cdot 100=10000\) entries?
Expected: here \(k(4+4+1)=9k\), so \(9\) and \(18\). For \(100\times 100\), \(k(201)<5000\) ⇒ \(k\le 24\).

title: Lecture 01 — Why linear algebra? Vectors as representations
text:
Fill in
An \(n\)-vector is an ordered list of \(\underline{\hspace{2.4cm}}\) numbers, written \[
x = (x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n)
\quad\text{or}\quad
x =
\begin{bmatrix}
x_1 \\
x_2 \\
\vdots \\
x_n
\end{bmatrix}.
\] The number \(n\) is the \(\underline{\hspace{2.4cm}}\) (or dimension) of \(x\). Each \(x_i\) is an \(\underline{\hspace{2.4cm}}\) of \(x\). In this course we index from \(i=1\) to \(i=n\) (Boyd’s convention).
Two \(n\)-vectors \(a\) and \(b\) are equal when \(\underline{\hspace{3.2cm}}\).
A scalar is \(\underline{\hspace{3.2cm}}\). The number \(x_3\) is a \(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\); the list \(x\) is a \(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\).
The zero vector \(0\) has \(\underline{\hspace{2.4cm}}\). The ones vector \(\mathbf{1}\) has \(\underline{\hspace{2.4cm}}\). The standard unit vector \(e_i\) has \(\underline{\hspace{3.6cm}}\).
In an application, we often keep a separate list of \(\underline{\hspace{2.4cm}}\) so that we know what each entry means and what \(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\) it has. Entries with different units are still allowed in one vector; comparing them as “the same kind of quantity” is \(\underline{\hspace{2.4cm}}\).

title: Lecture 01 — Why linear algebra? Vectors as representations
text:
Worked in class

title: Lecture 02 — Vector arithmetic and geometry
text:
Warm-up

title: Lecture 02 — Vector arithmetic and geometry
text:
Fill in
If \(a\) and \(b\) are \(n\)-vectors, the sum \(a+b\) is the \(n\)-vector whose \(i\)th entry is \(\underline{\hspace{2.8cm}}\). Addition is only defined when \(\underline{\hspace{3.0cm}}\).
The identity for addition is \(\underline{\hspace{1.6cm}}\): \(a+0=a\). The difference \(a-b\) is \(\underline{\hspace{2.4cm}}\).
If \(\beta\) is a scalar, the scalar–vector product \(\beta a\) is the \(n\)-vector whose \(i\)th entry is \(\underline{\hspace{2.4cm}}\). In particular, \((-1)a\) is written \(\underline{\hspace{1.2cm}}\).
Geometry in \(\mathbb{R}^2\): draw \(a\) as an arrow. Then \(\beta a\) with \(\beta>0\) points \(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\) and has length scaled by \(\underline{\hspace{1.4cm}}\). If \(\beta<0\), the arrow points \(\underline{\hspace{2.4cm}}\). The sum \(a+b\) can be drawn tip-to-tail or as the diagonal of a \(\underline{\hspace{2.4cm}}\).
The same formulas work entrywise in \(\mathbb{R}^3\); we just cannot sketch as easily on paper.
Adding a scalar to a vector is \(\underline{\hspace{2.4cm}}\) in the mathematics of this course (even if some software will do it). Concatenating \((1,2)\) with \((3,4)\) is also \(\underline{\hspace{2.4cm}}\) vector addition.

title: Lecture 02 — Vector arithmetic and geometry
text:

W2. Two rain gauges, in inches, over three days: \[
r = (0.40, 0, 1.10), \qquad s = (0.15, 0.20, 0.30).
\] Compute \(r+s\) and \(2r\). Why is \(r+(1,1)\) not a valid vector sum here? (These are 3-vectors: same arithmetic as in \(\mathbb{R}^2\), just one more entry.)
W3. Sanity check: can you form \((4,1)+(0,2,5)\)? Can you form \((18\text{ cm}, 4\text{ mm})+(1,1)\) as a meaningful measurement vector?

text:
Your turn

\begin{bmatrix} 4 \\ -1 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}
+
\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 3 \\ -2 \end{bmatrix}
\qquad\text{and}\qquad

\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0.5 \end{bmatrix}.

title: Lecture 03 — Linear combinations

Fill in
If \(a_1,\ldots,a_m\) are \(n\)-vectors and \(\beta_1,\ldots,\beta_m\) are scalars, the vector \[
\beta_1 a_1 + \cdots + \beta_m a_m
\] is a \(\underline{\hspace{2.8cm}}\) of \(a_1,\ldots,a_m\). The numbers \(\beta_1,\ldots,\beta_m\) are the \(\underline{\hspace{2.4cm}}\).
Any \(n\)-vector \(b\) can be written using the standard unit vectors: \[
b = \underline{\hspace{3.6cm}}.
\]
The sum \(a_1+\cdots+a_m\) is the linear combination whose coefficients are all \(\underline{\hspace{1.2cm}}\). The average is the linear combination whose coefficients are all \(\underline{\hspace{1.6cm}}\).
A coefficient \(\beta_i\) means \(\underline{\hspace{4.0cm}}\) in context (for example: how many copies of a recipe, how far to walk in a direction, how loud to mix a track).

title: Lecture 04 — Inner product
text:
Fill in — stack and slice
A stacked (or block) vector lists the entries of one vector after another. If \(b\) is an \(m\)-vector and \(c\) is an \(n\)-vector, then \[
(b, c) = (b_1,\ldots,b_m,\ c_1,\ldots,c_n)
\] is an \((m+n)\)-vector. A scalar can be stacked with a vector: if \(a\) is a 3-vector, then \((1,a)\) is a \(\underline{\hspace{1.6cm}}\)-vector with first entry \(1\), then \(a_1,a_2,a_3\).
Stacking is not vector addition: \((a,b)\) has length \(m+n\), not \(m\).
A slice (or subvector) takes a contiguous block of entries. Boyd’s notation \(x_{r:s}\) means the vector of entries \(x_r, x_{r+1}, \ldots, x_s\). It has length \(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\). The endpoints are inclusive.
Example: if \(z=(1,-1,2,0)\), then \(z_{2:3} = \underline{\hspace{2.4cm}}\).
If \(a\) and \(b\) are 10-vectors and \(c\) is a 20-vector, then \((a,b,c_{3:13})\) has length \(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\).

title: Lecture 04 — Inner product
text:
Fill in
For \(n\)-vectors \(a\) and \(b\), the inner product (or dot product) is the scalar \[
a^{\mathsf{T}}b = a_1 b_1 + a_2 b_2 + \cdots + a_n b_n = \sum_{i=1}^n \underline{\hspace{2.4cm}}.
\] It is only defined when \(a\) and \(b\) have the same \(\underline{\hspace{1.6cm}}\).
If \(w\) is a weight vector and \(x\) is a data vector (same length), then \(w^{\mathsf{T}}x\) is a \(\underline{\hspace{3.2cm}}\) of the entries of \(x\), using the weights in \(w\).
Geometrically in \(\mathbb{R}^2\) (and similarly in \(\mathbb{R}^3\)): if \(a^{\mathsf{T}}b>0\), the arrows point roughly the \(\underline{\hspace{2.4cm}}\) direction; if \(a^{\mathsf{T}}b<0\), they point roughly \(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\) directions; if \(a^{\mathsf{T}}b=0\), the vectors are \(\underline{\hspace{2.4cm}}\).
Two vectors with \(a^{\mathsf{T}}b=0\) are orthogonal (perpendicular). The inner product is commutative: \(a^{\mathsf{T}}b = \underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\).
The quantity \(a^{\mathsf{T}}a = a_1^2 + \cdots + a_n^2\) is always \(\underline{\hspace{1.6cm}}\) (never negative).

text:

W4. Three quiz parts have scores (out of 1): \[
g = (0.80,\ 0.90,\ 0.70),
\] with weights \[
w = (0.50,\ 0.30,\ 0.20).

W5. Morning wind displacements (east, north), in km/h: \[
a = (3, 1), \qquad b = (-1, 3).
\] Compute \(a^{\mathsf{T}}b\). Is it positive, negative, or zero? In one sentence, what does the sign tell you about how the two directions line up?

title: Lecture 04 — Inner product
text:
Your turn
Y1. Let \(a=(4,1,2)\) and \(b=(1,0,1)\) be shopping lists (apples, bread, milk). Write \((a,b)\) and state its length.
Y2. Let \(c=(10,12,11,14,13)\) be five daily counts. Find \(c_{2:4}\).
Y3. Compute \((2,-1)^{\mathsf{T}}(3,4)\) and \((1,0)^{\mathsf{T}}(0,1)\).
Y4. A café tracks daily sales in the order (espresso, milk, syrup): \[
x = (40,\ 30,\ 10),
\] with prices in dollars \[
p = (3,\ 2,\ 1).
\] What quantity does \(p^{\mathsf{T}}x\) represent? Compute it.
Y5. Two shopping lists, in the order (apples, bread, milk): \[
r = (2,\ 1,\ 3), \qquad s = (4,\ 2,\ 6).
\] Compute \(r^{\mathsf{T}}s\). Notice anything about \(r\) and \(s\)? If \(t=(1,0,-1)\), compute \(r^{\mathsf{T}}t\) and say whether \(r\) and \(t\) are orthogonal.






NoteAnswers (Your turn only)





Y1. \((a,b)=(4,1,2,1,0,1)\); length \(6\).
Y2. \(c_{2:4}=(12,11,14)\).
Y3. \((2,-1)^{\mathsf{T}}(3,4)=2\cdot 3+(-1)\cdot 4=2\). \((1,0)^{\mathsf{T}}(0,1)=0\) (orthogonal).
Y4. Total revenue in dollars: \(p^{\mathsf{T}}x=3\cdot 40+2\cdot 30+1\cdot 10=120+60+10=190\) dollars.
Y5. \(r^{\mathsf{T}}s=2\cdot 4+1\cdot 2+3\cdot 6=8+2+18=28\). Also \(s=2r\), so the lists are proportional (same “direction” in data space). \(r^{\mathsf{T}}t=2\cdot 1+1\cdot 0+3\cdot(-1)=2-3=-1\neq 0\), so \(r\) and \(t\) are not orthogonal.

Learning objectives

title: Lecture 05 — Linear and affine functions
text:
Fill in
A function \(f:\mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}\) is linear if for all \(n\)-vectors \(x,y\) and scalars \(\alpha,\beta\), \[
f(\alpha x + \beta y) = \alpha f(x) + \beta f(y).
\] This property is called \(\underline{\hspace{2.4cm}}\).
Equivalently, linear functions satisfy homogeneity \(f(\alpha x)=\alpha f(x)\) and additivity \(f(x+y)=f(x)+f(y)\).
Every linear function can be written as an inner product: \(f(x) = \underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\) for some fixed \(n\)-vector \(a\).
A function is affine if it has the form \(f(x) = a^{\mathsf{T}}x + b\) for some \(n\)-vector \(a\) and scalar \(b\). The number \(b\) is the \(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\) (or intercept).
Affine functions satisfy a restricted superposition rule: \(f(\alpha x + \beta y) = \alpha f(x) + \beta f(y)\) only when \(\alpha + \beta = \underline{\hspace{1.2cm}}\).
If \(b \neq 0\), the function \(f(x)=a^{\mathsf{T}}x+b\) is affine but \(\underline{\hspace{2.4cm}}\) linear.
The average \(\mathrm{avg}(x)=\frac{1}{n}(x_1+\cdots+x_n)\) is \(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\); the maximum entry \(\max(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\) is not (for \(n\geq 2\)).
A regression model \(\hat{y} = \beta^{\mathsf{T}}x + v\) predicts a scalar from features \(x\). The entry \(\beta_i\) tells how \(\hat{y}\) changes when feature \(x_i\) increases by one, holding other features fixed. The offset \(v\) is the predicted value when \(\underline{\hspace{2.8cm}}\).

title: Lecture 05 — Linear and affine functions
text:
Worked in class
W1. Classify each function below as linear, affine but not linear, or neither. If linear, write \(f(x)=a^{\mathsf{T}}x\).

\(f(x)=x_n-x_1\) (Boyd 2.1(b)).
\(f(x)=3x_1-2x_2+7\).
\(f(x)=\max(x_1,x_2)\) for \(n=2\).

W2. Superposition check. For \(f(x)=\max(x_1,x_2)\), let \(x=(1,-1)\), \(y=(-1,1)\), \(\alpha=\beta=\tfrac{1}{2}\). Compute \(f(\alpha x+\beta y)\) and \(\alpha f(x)+\beta f(y)\). What does this show?
W3. A 10-vector \(r\) stores course grades: \(r_1,\ldots,r_8\) are homework scores (0–10 each), \(r_9\) is midterm (0–120), \(r_10\) is final (0–160). Total score on 0–100 is 25% homework, 35% midterm, 40% final. Write \(s=w^{\mathsf{T}}r\) and give \(w\) (Boyd 1.10 style).
W4. Profit per unit is \(p=(4,2,-1)\) dollars for three items (item 3 is a loss leader). Monthly sales are \(s=(100,50,30)\) units. Total profit is \(p^{\mathsf{T}}s\) (Boyd 1.8). Compute it and interpret item 3’s sign.

title: Lecture 05 — Linear and affine functions
text:
Check yourself
C1. Boyd 2.1(a): \(f(x)=\max_k x_k - \min_k x_k\) (spread). Linear or not? One sentence why.
C2. Boyd 2.1(e): \(f(x)=x_n+(x_n-x_{n-1})\) (extrapolation). Linear or not? If linear, find \(a\) with \(f(x)=a^{\mathsf{T}}x\).
C3. Is \(g(x)=2x_1-x_3+5\) linear, affine, or neither? Write it as \(a^{\mathsf{T}}x+b\) if affine.
C4. Lachniet Ch. 1 Ex. 2(b): \(u=(2,-4,0)\), \(v=(3,1.5,-7)\). Find \(d=u^{\mathsf{T}}v\) (dot product). What does \(d=0\) suggest about direction?
C5. A café bill is \(f(x)=p^{\mathsf{T}}x\) with \(p=(3.50,2.00,1.25)\) and \(x=(2,1,0)\) (drinks ordered). Compute \(f(x)\) and state whether \(f\) is linear or affine.






NoteAnswers (Check yourself only)





C1. Not linear (nor affine): spread fails superposition (Boyd uses \(x=(1,-1)\), \(y=(-1,1)\), \(\alpha=\beta=1/2\)).
C2. Linear: \(f(x)=x_n+(x_n-x_{n-1})=2x_n-x_{n-1}\), so \(a=(0,\ldots,0,-1,2)\) with \(a_{n-1}=-1\), \(a_n=2\).
C3. Affine but not linear: \(a=(2,0,-1)^{\mathsf{T}}\), \(b=5\).
C4. \(d=2\cdot 3+(-4)\cdot 1.5+0=6-6=0\). The vectors are orthogonal (perpendicular in 3D).
C5. \(f(x)=3.50\cdot 2+2.00\cdot 1+1.25\cdot 0=9.00\) dollars. Linear (also affine with \(b=0\)).

title: Lecture 06 — Linear functions in applications

title: Lecture 06 — Linear functions in applications
text:
Fill in
An affine model \(f(x)=a^{\mathsf{T}}x+b\) often approximates a real quantity only over a limited range of inputs; outside that range the model may be \(\underline{\hspace{2.4cm}}\).
In a cost model \(c^{\mathsf{T}}q\), the entry \(c_i\) is the cost per unit of material \(i\). The total cost is a \(\underline{\hspace{2.4cm}}\) of the amounts \(q_i\).
In Boyd 1.14, \(f^{\mathsf{T}}h\) is sector exposure: net dollars invested in assets with \(f_i=1\). If \(f^{\mathsf{T}}h=0\), the portfolio is \(\underline{\hspace{2.4cm}}\) to that sector.
To pick the cheapest of \(K\) suppliers with price vectors \(p_1,\ldots,p_K\) for order \(q\), compare \(p_1^{\mathsf{T}}q,\ldots,p_K^{\mathsf{T}}q\) and choose the \(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\).
A regression model \(\hat{y}=\beta^{\mathsf{T}}x+v\) is useful when the relationship is roughly \(\underline{\hspace{2.4cm}}\) over the data range, but coefficients can be hard to interpret if features are \(\underline{\hspace{2.4cm}}\).

title: Lecture 06 — Linear functions in applications
text:
Worked in class
W1. A 30-question magazine quiz uses answers \(a_i\in\{1,2,3\}\) (Rarely, Sometimes, Often). Questions 1–15: Sometimes \(+1\), Often \(+2\). Questions 16–30: Sometimes \(+2\), Often \(+4\). Rarely adds 0. Write total score \(s=w^{\mathsf{T}}a+v\) (Boyd 2.6).
W2. Cash held in five currencies is \(c=(1000,500,-200,0,300)\) (USD, RMB, EUR, GBP, JPY). Exchange rates to USD are \(r=(1,0.14,1.08,1.27,0.0067)\). Total USD value is \(r^{\mathsf{T}}c\) (Boyd 1.12). Compute it (negative EUR is a liability).
W3. Three assets; pharma indicator \(f=(1,0,1)\). Portfolio \(h=(500,200,-100)\) dollars (short on asset 2). Compute exposure \(f^{\mathsf{T}}h\) (Boyd 1.14). In words, what does the sign mean?
W4. Order \(q=(10,5,20)\) of three materials. Supplier A prices \(p_A=(2,4,1)\); supplier B prices \(p_B=(3,2,2)\) per unit (Boyd 1.15). Which supplier is cheaper for the whole order? Compare \(p_A^{\mathsf{T}}q\) and \(p_B^{\mathsf{T}}q\).
W5. Processor temperature is affine in power: \(T=a^{\mathsf{T}}P+b\). Idle \(P=(10,10,10)\) gives \(T=30\). Full power on processor 1 only, \(P=(100,10,10)\), gives \(T=60\). Find \(a_1\) from those two readings (Boyd 2.2 setup).

title: Lecture 06 — Linear functions in applications
text:
Check yourself
C1. Two regression models for the same house: \(\hat{y}_A=200{,}000+120x_1+15{,}000x_2\) and \(\hat{y}_B=180{,}000+130x_1+18{,}000x_2\), where \(x_1\) is area (1000 ft²) and \(x_2\) is bedrooms. For \(x=(2,3)\), compute both predictions. Which predicts higher?
C2. Boyd 2.4 style: \(\varphi(1,1,0)=-1\), \(\varphi(-1,1,1)=1\), \(\varphi(1,-1,-1)=1\). Could \(\varphi\) be linear? Could it be affine? Brief reason.
C3. You must buy \(q=(4,2)\). Supplier 1: \(p_1=(5,3)\); supplier 2: \(p_2=(4,5)\). Which supplier wins on total cost \(p_k^{\mathsf{T}}q\)?
C4. A long-only portfolio (\(h_i\geq 0\)) is neutral to pharma (\(f^{\mathsf{T}}h=0\) with \(f_i\in\{0,1\}\)). In one sentence, what does that mean about pharma holdings?
C5. Name one reasonable limitation of using a linear model for café revenue \(p^{\mathsf{T}}x\) when \(x\) counts drinks sold.






NoteAnswers (Check yourself only)





C1. \(\hat{y}_A=200{,}000+120\cdot 2+15{,}000\cdot 3=245{,}240\). \(\hat{y}_B=180{,}000+130\cdot 2+18{,}000\cdot 3=248{,}260\). Model B predicts higher.
C2. Cannot be linear: if \(\varphi(x)=a^{\mathsf{T}}x\), the three given values force an inconsistent system for \(a\). Could be affine: many choices of \(a,b\) with \(\varphi(x)=a^{\mathsf{T}}x+b\) fit three input–output pairs.

title: Lecture 07 — Norm, distance, RMS, and variation
text:
Learning objectives
By the end of class, you should be able to:

Compute vector norms and distances.
Interpret norm and distance geometrically and contextually.
Relate norm to RMS and, where appropriate, variation around an average.
Use software to calculate distances in dimensions too large for hand computation.

title: Lecture 07 — Norm, distance, RMS, and variation
text:
Warm-up
Let \(u=(3,-4)\) and \(v=(0,5)\).

Compute \(u^{\mathsf{T}}u\) and \(\sqrt{u^{\mathsf{T}}u}\) by hand.
Without a calculator, which is larger: \(\lVert u\rVert\) or \(\lVert v\rVert\)? Brief reason.

title: Lecture 07 — Norm, distance, RMS, and variation
text:
Fill in
The Euclidean norm of an \(n\)-vector \(x\) is \[
\lVert x\rVert = \sqrt{x_1^2+\cdots+x_n^2} = \sqrt{\underline{\hspace{2.4cm}}}.
\] It measures the \(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\) of \(x\). For a scalar, \(\lVert x\rVert\) is the \(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\).
Key properties (same size vectors; \(\beta\) a scalar): - \(\lVert \beta x\rVert = \underline{\hspace{2.4cm}}\,\lVert x\rVert\) - \(\lVert x+y\rVert \leq \lVert x\rVert + \lVert y\rVert\) (triangle inequality) - \(\lVert x\rVert \geq 0\), and \(\lVert x\rVert=0\) only when \(x=\underline{\hspace{1.2cm}}\)
The RMS (root-mean-square) value is \[
\mathrm{rms}(x) = \frac{\lVert x\rVert}{\sqrt{n}} = \sqrt{\frac{x_1^2+\cdots+x_n^2}{n}}.
\] It describes a \(\underline{\hspace{2.4cm}}\) size of an entry, and is useful when comparing vectors of different \(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\).
The distance between \(n\)-vectors \(a\) and \(b\) is \[
\mathrm{dist}(a,b) = \lVert a-b\rVert.
\] Geometrically this is the length of the \(\underline{\hspace{2.4cm}}\) from \(a\) to \(b\). Two vectors are “close” when this distance is \(\underline{\hspace{1.6cm}}\) (relative to the application).
The average is \(\mathrm{avg}(x)=\frac{1}{n}\mathbf{1}^{\mathsf{T}}x\). The de-meaned vector is \(\tilde{x}=x-\mathrm{avg}(x)\mathbf{1}\). The standard deviation is \[
\mathrm{std}(x)=\mathrm{rms}(\tilde{x})=\frac{\lVert x-\mathrm{avg}(x)\mathbf{1}\rVert}{\sqrt{n}},
\] which measures typical \(\underline{\hspace{2.8cm}}\) of the entries from their average.
Boyd’s identity: \(\mathrm{rms}(x)^2 = \mathrm{avg}(x)^2 + \mathrm{std}(x)^2\).

title: Lecture 07 — Norm, distance, RMS, and variation
text:
Software (keep this page open)
In this course we use either Octave or Python for norms and distances.
Octave (column vectors are fine):
x = [3; -4; 0];
norm(x)                 % Euclidean norm
sqrt(x'*x)              % same idea via the inner product
y = [1; 2; -1];
norm(x-y)               % distance ||x-y||
Python (NumPy):
import numpy as np
x = np.array([3.0, -4.0, 0.0])
np.linalg.norm(x)       # Euclidean norm
np.sqrt(x @ x)          # same idea via the inner product
y = np.array([1.0, 2.0, -1.0])
np.linalg.norm(x - y)   # distance ||x-y||
Handy formulas (either language): - \(\mathrm{rms}(x)=\lVert x\rVert/\sqrt{n}\) - \(\mathrm{avg}(x)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_i x_i\) (Octave mean(x), Python np.mean(x)) - \(\mathrm{std}(x)\) in Boyd’s sense is the RMS of the de-meaned vector (population form with divisor \(n\), not \(n-1\))

Worked in class

W3. Boolean distance (Boyd 3.1). Suppose \(x\) and \(y\) are Boolean \(n\)-vectors (entries only \(0\) or \(1\)).

Therefore \(\lVert x-y\rVert=\sqrt{k}\) where \(k\) is that disagreement count. For \(x=(1,0,1,1,0)\) and \(y=(1,1,0,1,0)\), find \(k\) and \(\lVert x-y\rVert\).

W4. RMS, average, and standard deviation (Boyd 3.15 setup). Let \[
x=(2,4,4,6).
\] (a) Compute \(\mathrm{avg}(x)\), \(\lVert x\rVert\), \(\mathrm{rms}(x)\), the de-meaned vector \(\tilde{x}\), and \(\mathrm{std}(x)\).

Check Boyd’s identity \(\mathrm{rms}(x)^2=\mathrm{avg}(x)^2+\mathrm{std}(x)^2\).

W5. Feature scale changes nearest neighbor (Quiz 3 C1.2 style). Two features: area (in \(1000\) ft²) and bedrooms. Houses: \[
h_1=(1.6,\ 2),\qquad h_2=(1.5,\ 2),\qquad h_3=(1.6,\ 4).
\] (a) Compute \(\lVert h_1-h_2\rVert\) and \(\lVert h_1-h_3\rVert\). Which house is nearer to \(h_1\)?

Now measure area in square feet instead, so the vectors become \[
\tilde{h}_1=(1600,\ 2),\qquad \tilde{h}_2=(1500,\ 2),\qquad \tilde{h}_3=(1600,\ 4).
\] Compute \(\lVert\tilde{h}_1-\tilde{h}_2\rVert\) and \(\lVert\tilde{h}_1-\tilde{h}_3\rVert\). Which house is nearer to \(\tilde{h}_1\) now?
What changed, and why does Boyd warn about units on heterogeneous features?

title: Lecture 08 — Angle and similarity
text:
Learning objectives
By the end of class, you should be able to:

Compute cosine similarity or an angle between vectors.
Distinguish closeness in position from similarity in direction.
Choose an appropriate similarity measure for a stated purpose.
Explain why normalization may change a comparison.

title: Lecture 08 — Angle and similarity
text:
Warm-up
Let \(a=(1,0)\) and \(b=(1,1)\).

Compute \(a^{\mathsf{T}}b\), \(\lVert a\rVert\), and \(\lVert b\rVert\).
Without finding the angle in degrees, is \(\cos\theta = a^{\mathsf{T}}b/(\lVert a\rVert\lVert b\rVert)\) closer to \(1\), to \(0\), or to \(-1\)? What does that suggest about the directions?

title: Lecture 08 — Angle and similarity
text:
Fill in
For nonzero \(n\)-vectors \(a\) and \(b\), the angle \(\theta=\angle(a,b)\) satisfies \[
\cos\theta = \frac{a^{\mathsf{T}}b}{\lVert a\rVert\,\lVert b\rVert}, \qquad \theta\in[0,\pi].
\] The quantity \(\dfrac{a^{\mathsf{T}}b}{\lVert a\rVert\,\lVert b\rVert}\) is the cosine similarity.
Cauchy–Schwarz says \(|a^{\mathsf{T}}b|\leq\lVert a\rVert\lVert b\rVert\), so the cosine is always between \(\underline{\hspace{1.6cm}}\) and \(\underline{\hspace{1.6cm}}\).
Interpretation: - \(\theta\approx 0\) (cosine near \(1\)): directions nearly the \(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\) - \(\theta=\pi/2\) (cosine \(0\)): vectors are \(\underline{\hspace{2.4cm}}\) - \(\theta\approx\pi\) (cosine near \(-1\)): directions nearly \(\underline{\hspace{2.4cm}}\)
Distance \(\lVert a-b\rVert\) measures closeness of positions. Angle measures similarity of directions (independent of overall scale of each vector). Scaling \(a\) by a positive constant does \(\underline{\hspace{2.4cm}}\) change \(\angle(a,b)\).
A normalized (unit) vector is \(\hat{a}=a/\lVert a\rVert\), which has \(\lVert\hat{a}\rVert=\underline{\hspace{1.0cm}}\). Among unit vectors, smaller distance is equivalent to \(\underline{\hspace{2.8cm}}\) angle (Boyd 3.24(b)).

title: Lecture 08 — Angle and similarity
text:
Software
Octave:
a = [1; 0]; b = [1; 1];
cos_th = (a'*b)/(norm(a)*norm(b))
th_deg = acosd(cos_th)    % angle in degrees
Python:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1.0, 0.0]); b = np.array([1.0, 1.0])
cos_th = (a @ b) / (np.linalg.norm(a) * np.linalg.norm(b))
th_deg = np.degrees(np.arccos(np.clip(cos_th, -1, 1)))

x=(1,0),\qquad z_1=(2,0),\qquad z_2=(0.5,0.5).

text:
Check yourself

NoteAnswers (Check yourself only)





C1. \(a^{\mathsf{T}}b=12-12=0\), so cosine \(=0\). Yes, orthogonal (\(90^\circ\)).
C2. False. Example: \(a=(100,0)\), \(b=(101,0)\) are close in distance but that alone does not force a general claim for arbitrary nearby pairs that point opposite ways after a shift; clearer counterexample for “small distance \(\Rightarrow\) small angle”: take \(a=(0.01,0)\) and \(b=(-0.01,0)\) — distance \(0.02\) is small, but angle is \(180^\circ\).
C3. Documents can have very different lengths (total word counts). Angle / cosine ignores overall scale and focuses on the pattern of which words appear together.
C4. Octave: (a'*b)/(norm(a)*norm(b)). Python: (a @ b)/(np.linalg.norm(a)*np.linalg.norm(b)).

title: Lecture 09 — Nearest neighbors
text:
Warm-up
Patients as 2-vectors (fever °F above 98.6, cough score 0–10): \[
p=(1.2,\ 3),\quad q=(0.1,\ 8),\quad r=(1.0,\ 4).
\] A new patient is \(x=(1.1,\ 3.5)\). Which of \(p,q,r\) is nearest to \(x\) in Euclidean distance? Compute the three distances.

title: Lecture 09 — Nearest neighbors
text:
Fill in
Given candidates \(z_1,\ldots,z_m\) and a query \(x\), a (distance) nearest neighbor is any \(z_j\) with \[
\lVert x-z_j\rVert \leq \lVert x-z_i\rVert \quad\text{for all }i.
\] In words: the candidate with \(\underline{\hspace{2.8cm}}\) Euclidean distance to \(x\).
An angle nearest neighbor minimizes \(\angle(x,z_i)\) instead (equivalently maximizes cosine similarity when angles are in \([0,\pi]\)).
Feature vectors often mix units (age, dollars, counts). Then \(\lVert x-y\rVert^2\) adds \(\underline{\hspace{3.2cm}}\) of entrywise differences, so a large-scale feature can \(\underline{\hspace{2.4cm}}\) the distance. Remedies include choosing units carefully, \(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\) features, or using a \(\underline{\hspace{2.4cm}}\) (Boyd 3.28).
Choose Euclidean distance when “close in feature space” means similar \(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\). Choose angle/cosine when overall \(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\) should not matter (documents, some sensors).

title: Lecture 09 — Nearest neighbors
text:
Software
Octave — distances from x to rows of a matrix Z (one candidate per row):
x = [1.1; 3.5];
Z = [1.2, 3; 0.1, 8; 1.0, 4];   % each row a candidate
d = sqrt(sum((Z - x').^2, 2))  % 3 distances
[~, j] = min(d)                % nearest index
Python:
import numpy as np
x = np.array([1.1, 3.5])
Z = np.array([[1.2, 3.0], [0.1, 8.0], [1.0, 4.0]])
d = np.linalg.norm(Z - x, axis=1)
j = np.argmin(d)

Learning objectives

title: Lecture 10 — Clustering and \(k\)-means
text:
Warm-up
Six points in \(\mathbb{R}^2\): \[
(0,0),\ (0,1),\ (1,0),\quad (5,5),\ (5,6),\ (6,5).
\] By eye, into how many natural groups do they fall? Suggest a representative (center) for each group.

title: Lecture 10 — Clustering and \(k\)-means
text:
Fill in
Clustering partitions \(N\) vectors \(x_1,\ldots,x_N\) into \(k\) groups so that vectors in the same group are \(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\) to each other (small pairwise distances).
A group representative (centroid, when we use the mean) \(z_j\) is a vector that stands for cluster \(j\). The basic clustering objective sums squared distances from each point to its group’s representative: \[
J^{\mathrm{clust}} = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N \lVert x_i - z_{c_i}\rVert^2,
\] where \(c_i\) is the cluster index of \(x_i\).
\(k\)-means alternates two steps:

Assignment: given representatives \(z_1,\ldots,z_k\), set each \(c_i\) to the index of the \(\underline{\hspace{2.8cm}}\) \(z_j\) to \(x_i\).
Update: given assignments, replace each \(z_j\) by the \(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\) of the points currently in cluster \(j\).

The algorithm is a \(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\): different initial \(z_j\) can yield different final clusterings. Feature \(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\) and the choice of \(k\) also change the result.

title: Lecture 10 — Clustering and \(k\)-means
text:

\] Representatives \(z_1=(1,1)\), \(z_2=(7,1)\). Assign each \(x_i\) to the nearest \(z_j\). List the two clusters.
W3. One update step. Using your clusters from W2, replace each \(z_j\) by the mean of its points. What are the new centroids?
W4. Interpret a centroid. If a cluster of temperature vectors has centroid \((54,53,55)\) for three morning hours, what does that vector mean?
W5. Sensitivity. Same four points as W2, but start with \(z_1=(0,1)\), \(z_2=(0,0)\). After one assignment, what goes wrong if both points near the origin grab almost everything? (One sentence on initialization.)

Interpret dependence as redundant information.
Explain why redundancy matters in data, measurement, and computation.

title: Lecture 12 — Linear dependence as redundancy
text:
Warm-up
Let \(a=(1,0)\), \(b=(0,1)\), and \(c=(1,1)\).

Find scalars \(\alpha,\beta\) (not both zero is fine) so that \(c=\alpha a+\beta b\).
In one sentence: is knowing \(c\) “new information” once you already know \(a\) and \(b\)?

title: Lecture 12 — Linear dependence as redundancy
text:
Fill in
A list of \(n\)-vectors \(a_1,\ldots,a_k\) is linearly dependent if there exist scalars \(\beta_1,\ldots,\beta_k\), not all zero, such that \[
\beta_1 a_1+\cdots+\beta_k a_k = \underline{\hspace{1.2cm}}.
\] Any such nontrivial combination equal to zero is a dependence relation.
The list is linearly independent if the only solution of \(\beta_1 a_1+\cdots+\beta_k a_k=0\) is \(\beta_1=\cdots=\beta_k=\underline{\hspace{1.0cm}}\).
Equivalent picture: the list is dependent if (and only if) at least one vector is a \(\underline{\hspace{2.8cm}}\) of the others (or the list contains the zero vector).
Redundancy: if the vectors are features, sensors, or columns of data and they are dependent, then at least one measurement can be \(\underline{\hspace{2.4cm}}\) from the others — it does not add a new independent piece of information.
A single nonzero vector is always \(\underline{\hspace{2.4cm}}\). Two vectors are dependent iff one is a \(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\) of the other.

title: Lecture 12 — Linear dependence as redundancy
text:
Worked in class
W1. Independent or dependent? For each list in \(\mathbb{R}^2\), decide and give a one-line reason.

\((1,0),\ (0,1)\)
\((2,4),\ (1,2)\)
\((1,1),\ (1,-1),\ (0,2)\)

W2. Construct a dependence relation. For \(u=(1,2)\), \(v=(2,1)\), \(w=(3,3)\), find \(\beta_1,\beta_2,\beta_3\) not all zero with \(\beta_1 u+\beta_2 v+\beta_3 w=0\). (Hint: notice \(w=u+v\).)
W3. Sensors. Three temperature sensors report daily averages as vectors of length \(7\). Sensor C always equals (Sensor A \(+\) Sensor B)\(/2\). Are the three weekly report vectors dependent? What does that mean for “how many independent sensors” you really have?
W4. Features. Customer vectors (age, income, spending). Someone adds a fourth feature “age in months” \(=12\times\) age. Does the new feature add independent information for linear models that use these coordinates?
W5. Zero vector. Why is any list that includes \(0\) automatically dependent?

title: Lecture 12 — Linear dependence as redundancy
text:
Check yourself
C1. Are \((1,0,0)\), \((0,1,0)\), \((0,0,1)\) independent in \(\mathbb{R}^3\)? Brief reason.
C2. Find a dependence relation for \((1,1)\), \((2,2)\), \((0,1)\).
C3. True or false: if every pair in a list of three vectors is independent, then the whole list is independent.
C4. In one sentence: why might redundant features waste storage or confuse nearest-neighbor distance?
C5. Give one independent list of two vectors in \(\mathbb{R}^2\) and one dependent list of two vectors in \(\mathbb{R}^2\).






NoteAnswers (Check yourself only)





C1. Yes. If \(\beta_1(1,0,0)+\beta_2(0,1,0)+\beta_3(0,0,1)=0\), then \((\beta_1,\beta_2,\beta_3)=0\), so only the trivial combination works.
C2. Example: \((1,1)\) and \((2,2)\) are multiples, so \(2\cdot(1,1)+(-1)\cdot(2,2)+0\cdot(0,1)=0\). (Any nontrivial relation that uses that fact is fine.)
C3. False. Counterexample: \((1,0)\), \((0,1)\), \((1,1)\) — each pair is independent, but the three are dependent because \((1,1)=(1,0)+(0,1)\).
C4. A redundant coordinate can overweight that direction in Euclidean distance (or store duplicated information) without adding a new independent signal.
C5. Independent example: \((1,0),\ (0,1)\). Dependent example: \((1,2),\ (2,4)\).

Learning objectives

title: Lecture 13 — Span, independence, and subspaces
text:
Warm-up

title: Lecture 13 — Span, independence, and subspaces
text:
Fill in
The span of vectors \(a_1,\ldots,a_k\) is the set of all linear combinations \[
\operatorname{span}\{a_1,\ldots,a_k\}
  = \{\, \beta_1 a_1+\cdots+\beta_k a_k \mid \beta_i\in\mathbb{R} \,\}.
\] So \(v\) lies in the span iff the equation \(\beta_1 a_1+\cdots+\beta_k a_k=v\) has \(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\).
Geometry (in \(\mathbb{R}^2\) or \(\mathbb{R}^3\)):

Span of one nonzero vector: a \(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\) through the origin.
Span of two non-parallel vectors in \(\mathbb{R}^3\): a \(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\) through the origin.
Span of the standard basis of \(\mathbb{R}^n\): all of \(\underline{\hspace{1.4cm}}\).

A subspace of \(\mathbb{R}^n\) is a nonempty set \(V\) closed under addition and scalar multiplication (equivalently: closed under linear combinations). Every subspace contains \(\underline{\hspace{1.0cm}}\).
Spans are always subspaces. A line or plane that does not pass through the origin is \(\underline{\hspace{2.4cm}}\) a subspace (it fails to contain \(0\), or fails closure under scaling).
Independence vs span: an independent list that spans \(V\) will be called a basis of \(V\) next class. Today, focus on “can I build \(v\) from these vectors?”

title: Lecture 13 — Span, independence, and subspaces
text:
Worked in class
W1. Membership. Let \(a=(1,1)\) and \(b=(1,-1)\).

Is \(v=(2,0)\) in \(\operatorname{span}\{a,b\}\)? Find coefficients or explain why not.
Is \(w=(1,0,0)\) in \(\operatorname{span}\{(1,1,0),(0,1,1)\}\) inside \(\mathbb{R}^3\)?

W2. Geometry. Sketch in \(\mathbb{R}^2\): \(\operatorname{span}\{(2,1)\}\) and \(\operatorname{span}\{(1,0),(0,1)\}\).
W3. Subspace check. Which of the following are subspaces of \(\mathbb{R}^2\)? Brief reason.

All vectors \((x,y)\) with \(y=3x\).
All vectors \((x,y)\) with \(y=3x+1\).
The single point \(\{(0,0)\}\).
All vectors with \(\lVert(x,y)\rVert=1\) (the unit circle).

W4. Dependent generators. Let \(a=(1,0)\), \(b=(2,0)\), \(c=(0,1)\). Explain why \(\operatorname{span}\{a,b,c\}=\operatorname{span}\{a,c\}\). What does that say about redundant generators?
W5. Application. Two feature directions \(f_1=\)“morning temperature pattern” and \(f_2=\)“afternoon pattern” as \(24\)-vectors. What does it mean if a third pattern \(g\) lies in \(\operatorname{span}\{f_1,f_2\}\)?

title: Lecture 13 — Span, independence, and subspaces
text:
Check yourself
C1. Complete: \(v\in\operatorname{span}\{a,b\}\) means \(v=\underline{\hspace{3.2cm}}\) for some scalars.
C2. Is \((3,3)\) in \(\operatorname{span}\{(1,1)\}\)? Coefficients if yes.
C3. True or false: every subspace of \(\mathbb{R}^n\) is a span of some list of vectors.
C4. Why is the set of vectors with first entry equal to \(1\) not a subspace of \(\mathbb{R}^2\)?
C5. Give a vector in \(\mathbb{R}^2\) that is not in \(\operatorname{span}\{(1,2)\}\).






NoteAnswers (Check yourself only)





C1. \(v=\alpha a+\beta b\) (any equivalent wording).
C2. Yes. \((3,3)=3\cdot(1,1)\).
C3. True (in \(\mathbb{R}^n\) every subspace has a basis, hence is a span). For this course it is enough to know that the subspaces we meet are spans.
C4. It does not contain \(0\) (first entry would be \(0\)), or equivalently it is not closed under scaling.
C5. Example: \((1,0)\), or \((2,1)\), or any vector not a multiple of \((1,2)\).

text:
Learning objectives
By the end of class, you should be able to:

Explain what a basis accomplishes.

Use linear combination, span, subspace, independence, basis, and dimension accurately.
Recognize an orthonormal collection.

title: Lecture 14 — Basis, dimension, and orthonormal vectors
text:
Warm-up
Let \(a=(1,0)\) and \(b=(1,1)\).

Is \(\{a,b\}\) independent? Does it span \(\mathbb{R}^2\)?
Can every \(v=(v_1,v_2)\) be written uniquely as \(\alpha a+\beta b\)? (Try \(v=(2,3)\).)

title: Lecture 14 — Basis, dimension, and orthonormal vectors
text:
Fill in
A basis of a subspace \(V\) is a list of vectors that is both

\(\underline{\hspace{2.8cm}}\) (no redundancy), and
a \(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\) set for \(V\) (every vector in \(V\) is a linear combination of the list).

What a basis accomplishes: every \(v\in V\) has coefficients (coordinates) with respect to the basis — a unique recipe \(v=\beta_1 a_1+\cdots+\beta_k a_k\).
The dimension of \(V\) is the number of vectors in \(\underline{\hspace{2.4cm}}\) of \(V\). (All bases of \(V\) have the same length.)
Examples:

\(\dim\mathbb{R}^n=\underline{\hspace{1.0cm}}\) (standard basis \(e_1,\ldots,e_n\)).
A line through the origin through a nonzero \(a\) has dimension \(\underline{\hspace{1.0cm}}\).
A plane through the origin spanned by two independent vectors has dimension \(\underline{\hspace{1.0cm}}\).

An orthonormal list \(q_1,\ldots,q_k\) satisfies \(q_i^{\mathsf{T}}q_j=\underline{\hspace{1.0cm}}\) if \(i\neq j\), and \(\lVert q_i\rVert=\underline{\hspace{1.0cm}}\).
For an orthonormal basis of a subspace, the coefficients of \(v\) are especially simple: \[
\beta_i = \underline{\hspace{2.4cm}}
\] (inner products — no linear system to solve). That is why orthonormal coordinates are convenient for measurement and reconstruction.

title: Lecture 14 — Basis, dimension, and orthonormal vectors
text:
Worked in class
W1. Basis or not? For each list, is it a basis of \(\mathbb{R}^2\)? If not, say whether it fails independence, spanning, or both.

\((1,0),\ (0,1)\)
\((1,1),\ (2,2)\)
\((1,0),\ (0,1),\ (1,1)\)
\((1,1)\) alone

W2. Dimension. Let \(V=\operatorname{span}\{(1,2,0),(2,4,0),(0,0,1)\}\). Find a basis of \(V\) and \(\dim V\).
W3. Vocabulary drill. Fill each blank with one of: linear combination, span, subspace, independent, dependent, basis, dimension.

\(\operatorname{span}\{a,b\}\) is always a \(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\) of \(\mathbb{R}^n\).
If \(c=2a-b\), then \(\{a,b,c\}\) is \(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\).
A \(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\) of \(V\) is an independent spanning list for \(V\).

W4. Orthonormal check. Which of these pairs in \(\mathbb{R}^2\) is orthonormal?

\((1,0),\ (0,1)\)
\((1,1)/\sqrt{2},\ (1,-1)/\sqrt{2}\)
\((1,0),\ (1,1)\)

W5. Orthonormal coordinates. Let \(q_1=(1,0)\) and \(q_2=(0,1)\) (standard basis — already orthonormal). For \(v=(3,-2)\), what are \(\beta_1=q_1^{\mathsf{T}}v\) and \(\beta_2=q_2^{\mathsf{T}}v\)? Check \(v=\beta_1 q_1+\beta_2 q_2\).
W6 (time permitting). Gram–Schmidt idea. From independent \(a_1=(1,1)\) and \(a_2=(1,0)\), form \(q_1=a_1/\lVert a_1\rVert\), then subtract from \(a_2\) its projection onto \(q_1\), and normalize. (Board sketch only.)

title: Lecture 14 — Basis, dimension, and orthonormal vectors
text:
Check yourself
C1. A basis of a subspace is a list that is \(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\) and \(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\).
C2. \(\dim\operatorname{span}\{(1,0,0),(0,1,0)\}=\underline{\hspace{1.0cm}}\).
C3. True or false: every spanning list for \(V\) is a basis of \(V\).
C4. If \(\{q_1,q_2\}\) is orthonormal and \(v=\beta_1 q_1+\beta_2 q_2\), then \(\beta_1=\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\).
C5. Why are orthonormal coordinates nicer than coordinates in a skewed basis like \((1,0),\ (1,1)\)?






NoteAnswers (Check yourself only)





C1. independent and spanning (for that subspace).
C2. \(2\)
C3. False. Spanning lists can be dependent (too many vectors); a basis cannot.
C4. \(\beta_1=q_1^{\mathsf{T}}v\)
C5. Coefficients are inner products (no \(2\times 2\) solve); lengths and angles stay easy because the basis vectors are unit and orthogonal.

title: Lecture 18 — Matrices as data and structured objects
text:
Warm-up
Let \[
A =
\begin{bmatrix}
2 & -1 & 0 \\
4 & 3 & 1
\end{bmatrix}.
\]

What are the dimensions of \(A\)? Is it tall, wide, or square?
What is \(A_{23}\)? What is the second column of \(A\) as a vector?

title: Lecture 18 — Matrices as data and structured objects
text:
Fill in
An \(m\times n\) matrix is a rectangular array with \(\underline{\hspace{1.4cm}}\) rows and \(\underline{\hspace{1.4cm}}\) columns. The entry in row \(i\) and column \(j\) is written \(A_{ij}\) (Boyd: indices start at \(1\)).
We can view \(A\) as its \(n\) columns (each an \(m\)-vector) side by side, or as its \(m\) rows (each an \(n\)-row-vector) stacked.
Examples of “matrix as data”:

An image: pixel values in a grid.
A table: locations \(\times\) days, or customers \(\times\) products.
A relation / directed graph: adjacency matrix with \(A_{ij}=1\) when there is an edge from \(j\) to \(i\) (Boyd’s convention).

Transpose. \((A^{\mathsf{T}})_{ij}=\underline{\hspace{1.6cm}}\). If \(A\) is \(m\times n\), then \(A^{\mathsf{T}}\) is \(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\).
Addition and scaling. \(A+B\) and \(\beta A\) are entrywise (same size required for addition).
Special matrices (square, unless noted):



Name
Pattern




Zero \(0\)
all entries \(\underline{\hspace{1.0cm}}\)


Identity \(I\)
\(1\)s on the diagonal, \(0\)s elsewhere


Diagonal
off-diagonal entries are \(\underline{\hspace{1.0cm}}\)


Upper triangular
zeros \(\underline{\hspace{2.4cm}}\) the diagonal


Symmetric
\(A^{\mathsf{T}}=\underline{\hspace{1.0cm}}\)


Sparse
\(\underline{\hspace{2.8cm}}\) of the entries are nonzero



Practical consequence: structure (sparsity, triangularity, symmetry) often means cheaper storage or faster algorithms — we take advantage of the pattern instead of treating every entry as generic.

title: Lecture 18 — Matrices as data and structured objects
text:
Worked in class
W1. Dimensions and pieces. Let \[
B =
\begin{bmatrix}
1 & 0 & -2 \\
3 & 4 & 5 \\
0 & 1 & 1
\end{bmatrix}.
\] Give \(B_{31}\), the third row, and the first column. Is \(B\) square?
W2. Data matrix. Three weather stations record (high °F, low °F) for one day. Station 1: \((62,48)\); station 2: \((58,45)\); station 3: \((65,50)\). Write a \(2\times 3\) matrix \(W\) whose columns are the station readings. What does \(W_{12}\) mean?
W3. Arithmetic. With \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\0&-1\end{bmatrix},\quad
C=\begin{bmatrix}0&1\\3&2\end{bmatrix},
\] compute \(A+C\), \(2A\), and \(A^{\mathsf{T}}\).
W4. Structure check. For each matrix, name every special type that applies (zero / identity / diagonal / triangular / symmetric / sparse — sparse is judgment call for tiny examples).

\(\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\0&1\end{bmatrix}\)
\(\begin{bmatrix}2&0\\0&-3\end{bmatrix}\)
\(\begin{bmatrix}1&4\\0&2\end{bmatrix}\)
\(\begin{bmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{bmatrix}\)

W5. Why structure matters. An \(n\times n\) identity matrix has how many nonzero entries? Density \(nnz/(n^2)\)? Why might software store only the nonzeros of a sparse customer-purchase matrix?

title: Lecture 18 — Matrices as data and structured objects
text:
Your turn
Y1. Let \[
M =
\begin{bmatrix}
0 & 2 & 1 \\
-1 & 3 & 4
\end{bmatrix}.
\] Dimensions? \(M_{21}\)? Second column? Is \(M\) tall or wide?
Y2. A tiny directed graph on nodes \(\{1,2,3\}\) has edges \(2\to 1\), \(1\to 3\), and \(3\to 2\). Using Boyd’s convention (\(A_{ij}=1\) means edge from \(j\) to \(i\)), write the \(3\times 3\) adjacency matrix.
Y3. With \(A=\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\2&3\end{bmatrix}\), compute \(A+A^{\mathsf{T}}\). Is the result symmetric? Why?
Y4. True or false, with a one-line reason: every diagonal matrix is symmetric.






NoteAnswers (Your turn only)





Y1. \(2\times 3\); wide. \(M_{21}=-1\). Second column \((2,3)\).
Y2. \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}
0 & 1 & 0 \\
0 & 0 & 1 \\
1 & 0 & 0
\end{bmatrix}
\] (edge \(2\to 1\) puts a \(1\) in row 1, column 2; \(1\to 3\) puts a \(1\) in row 3, column 1; \(3\to 2\) puts a \(1\) in row 2, column 3).
Y3. \(A+A^{\mathsf{T}}=\begin{bmatrix}2&2\\2&6\end{bmatrix}\), which equals its transpose, so yes — sum of a matrix and its transpose is always symmetric.
Y4. True. Off-diagonal entries are already \(0=0\), so \(A^{\mathsf{T}}=A\).

title: Lecture 19 — Matrix-vector multiplication
text:
Warm-up
Let \(a=(1,2)\) and \(b=(-1,1)\). Compute \(2a-3b\). (This is the same skill as “columns of \(A\) times entries of \(x\).”)

title: Lecture 19 — Matrix-vector multiplication
text:
Fill in
If \(A\) is \(m\times n\) and \(x\) is an \(n\)-vector, the product \(y=Ax\) is an \(\underline{\hspace{1.4cm}}\)-vector.
Row view. The \(i\)th entry of \(Ax\) is the inner product of \(x\) with the \(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\) of \(A\): \[
y_i = (\text{row }i)^{\mathsf{T}}x.
\]
Column view (main story). If \(a_1,\ldots,a_n\) are the columns of \(A\), then \[
Ax = x_1 a_1 + x_2 a_2 + \cdots + x_n a_n.
\] So \(Ax\) is a \(\underline{\hspace{2.8cm}}\) of the columns of \(A\), with coefficients from \(x\).
Dimensions: \(A\) maps inputs in \(\mathbb{R}^{\underline{\hspace{0.8cm}}}\) to outputs in \(\mathbb{R}^{\underline{\hspace{0.8cm}}}\). Thinking of \(A\) as a machine: feed in \(x\), get out \(Ax\).
Special cases: \(Ix=x\); \(0x=0\); if \(A=\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_n)\), then \(Ax=(\lambda_1 x_1,\ldots,\lambda_n x_n)\).

title: Lecture 19 — Matrix-vector multiplication
text:
Worked in class
W1. Compute by hand. \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}1&2&0\\ -1&3&1\end{bmatrix},\quad
x=\begin{bmatrix}2\\ 1\\ -1\end{bmatrix}.
\] Find \(Ax\) using both the row-inner-product view and the column-combination view.
W2. Same \(A\), different \(x\). Without recomputing from scratch: if you already know \(Ax\) from W1, what is \(A(2x)\)? What is \(A(x+e_1)\) if \(e_1=(1,0,0)\)? (Use linearity / columns.)
W3. Input-output story. A \(2\times 2\) matrix \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}0.9&0.2\\ 0.1&0.8\end{bmatrix}
\] sends (urban, rural) population fractions today to tomorrow. If \(x=(0.6,0.4)\), compute \(Ax\) and interpret the two output entries.
W4. Dimension mismatch. Can you form \(Ax\) if \(A\) is \(3\times 2\) and \(x\) is a \(3\)-vector? What size must \(x\) be?

title: Lecture 19 — Matrix-vector multiplication
text:
Your turn
Y1. Compute \[
\begin{bmatrix}
2 & -1 \\
0 & 3 \\
1 & 1
\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}
4 \\ -2
\end{bmatrix}.
\]
Y2. Let \(A\) have columns \(a_1=(1,0,1)\) and \(a_2=(0,1,1)\). Write \(A\) explicitly. For \(x=(3,-2)\), express \(Ax\) as a linear combination of \(a_1,a_2\), then evaluate.
Y3. True or false: if \(A\) is \(m\times n\), then \(Ax\) is always in the span of the columns of \(A\).
Y4. A sensor turns a \(3\)-vector of raw readings \(x\) into a \(2\)-vector of summaries via \(Ax\). What are the dimensions of \(A\)? In one sentence, what do the columns of \(A\) mean?






NoteAnswers (Your turn only)





Y1. \((2)(4)+(-1)(-2)=10\); \((0)(4)+(3)(-2)=-6\); \((1)(4)+(1)(-2)=2\). So \(Ax=(10,-6,2)\).
Y2. \(A=\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\0&1\\1&1\end{bmatrix}\). \(Ax=3a_1-2a_2=(3,-2,1)\).
Y3. True. By the column interpretation, \(Ax\) is always a linear combination of the columns.
Y4. \(A\) is \(2\times 3\). The \(j\)th column is the summary \(2\)-vector produced when the input is the standard unit vector \(e_j\) (effect of “only feature \(j\) active”).

title: Lecture 20 — Transforming space
text:
Learning objectives
By the end of class, you should be able to:

Predict the effect of scaling, reflection, shear, and rotation matrices.
Apply matrices to many 2D or 3D points at once.
Plot and compare original and transformed objects.
Adapt a short program that implements a transformation.
Interpret a matrix as a coordinate or physical-space transformation.

title: Lecture 20 — Transforming space
text:
Warm-up
Predict, without multiplying: where does \(A=\operatorname{diag}(2,1/2)\) send the point \((1,1)\)? Sketch the original and image roughly.

title: Lecture 20 — Transforming space
text:
Fill in
Many geometric maps on \(\mathbb{R}^2\) (or \(\mathbb{R}^3\)) are matrix-vector products \(y=Ax\).
Finding the matrix. The \(j\)th column of \(A\) is what the map does to \(\underline{\hspace{1.2cm}}\). So apply the geometry to \(e_1,e_2\) (and \(e_3\) in 3D) to read off columns.
Common \(2\times 2\) examples:

Scaling / dilation: \(A=\operatorname{diag}(s_1,s_2)\) stretches the axes by \(s_1,s_2\).
Rotation counterclockwise by \(\theta\): \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}\cos\theta&-\sin\theta\\ \sin\theta&\cos\theta\end{bmatrix}.
\]
Reflection through a line through the origin; shear (e.g. \(\begin{bmatrix}1&k\\0&1\end{bmatrix}\)).

Many points at once. If columns of \(X\) are points, then \(AX\) applies the same map to every column.
Change of coordinates (3D idea). Body-fixed vs earth-fixed frames: \(x_{\mathrm{earth}}=p+Qx_{\mathrm{body}}\), where columns of \(Q\) are the body axes expressed in earth coordinates.

title: Lecture 20 — Transforming space
text:
Worked in class
W1. Build from \(e_1,e_2\). Reflection through the \(x_1\)-axis sends \((1,0)\mapsto(1,0)\) and \((0,1)\mapsto(0,-1)\). Write \(A\). Check \(A(2,3)\).
W2. Rotation. For \(\theta=90^\circ=\pi/2\), write the rotation matrix and compute \(A(1,0)\) and \(A(0,1)\). Does that match “\(90^\circ\) counterclockwise”?
W3. Many points. Let \(X=\begin{bmatrix}1&0&1\\0&1&1\end{bmatrix}\) (three corners of a right triangle). With \(A=\operatorname{diag}(2,1)\), compute \(AX\) and describe the image.
W4 (time permitting). Shear \(A=\begin{bmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{bmatrix}\). Where do \((1,0)\) and \((0,1)\) go? Sketch the unit square’s image.

title: Lecture 20 — Transforming space
text:
Your turn
Y1. Reflection through the \(x_2\)-axis: write \(A\) by tracking \(e_1\) and \(e_2\), then compute \(A(3,-1)\).
Y2. Rotation by \(180^\circ\): write \(A\) and apply it to \((2,1)\).
Y3. True or false: every \(2\times 2\) matrix represents a rotation of the plane.






NoteAnswers (Your turn only)





Y1. \(e_1\mapsto(-1,0)\), \(e_2\mapsto(0,1)\), so \(A=\begin{bmatrix}-1&0\\0&1\end{bmatrix}\). \(A(3,-1)=(-3,-1)\).
Y2. \(A=\begin{bmatrix}-1&0\\0&-1\end{bmatrix}=-I\). \(A(2,1)=(-2,-1)\).
Y3. False. Scaling, shear, projections, and many other maps are also \(2\times 2\) matrices; rotations are a special family.

title: Lecture 21 — Systems and \(Ax=b\)
text:
Learning objectives
By the end of class, you should be able to:

Translate equations or contextual constraints into \(Ax=b\).
Interpret \(Ax=b\) as asking whether \(b\) belongs to the span of the columns of \(A\).
Classify systems as square, underdetermined, or overdetermined.
Anticipate circumstances producing zero, one, or many solutions.

title: Lecture 21 — Systems and \(Ax=b\)
text:
Warm-up
Rewrite the system \[
\begin{aligned}
x_1 - 2x_2 &= 3 \\
2x_1 + x_2 &= 1
\end{aligned}
\] as \(Ax=b\). What are \(A\), \(x\), and \(b\)? Is \(b\) in the span of the columns of \(A\)? (You may decide by solving or by a short span argument.)

title: Lecture 21 — Systems and \(Ax=b\)
text:
Fill in
A linear system with \(m\) equations in \(n\) unknowns can be written \(Ax=b\), where \(A\) is \(\underline{\hspace{1.6cm}}\), \(x\) is an \(\underline{\hspace{1.2cm}}\)-vector, and \(b\) is an \(\underline{\hspace{1.2cm}}\)-vector.
Column view. Solving \(Ax=b\) asks: is \(b\) a \(\underline{\hspace{2.4cm}}\) of the columns of \(A\)? Equivalently: does \(b\) lie in \(\operatorname{span}\{\text{columns of }A\}\)?
Shape vocabulary (compare \(m\) equations to \(n\) unknowns):








Name
Relation
Typical intuition




Square
\(m=\underline{\hspace{0.8cm}}\)
Often one solution, but not always


Overdetermined
\(m>\underline{\hspace{0.8cm}}\)
Often \(\underline{\hspace{1.6cm}}\) (too many constraints)


Underdetermined
\(m<\underline{\hspace{0.8cm}}\)
Often \(\underline{\hspace{1.6cm}}\) (free variables)



These are tendencies, not guarantees: a square system can be inconsistent or have infinitely many solutions; an overdetermined system can still be consistent.
Possible outcomes for \(Ax=b\):

No solution — \(b\) is \(\underline{\hspace{2.8cm}}\) the column space.
Unique solution — \(b\) is in the column space in exactly \(\underline{\hspace{1.2cm}}\) way.
Infinitely many solutions — \(b\) is in the column space in \(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\) ways (free parameters).

title: Lecture 21 — Systems and \(Ax=b\)
text:
Worked in class
W1. Matrix form. Three unknowns \(x_1,x_2,x_3\): \[
\begin{aligned}
x_1 + x_2 &= 4 \\
x_2 - x_3 &= 1 \\
2x_1 + x_3 &= 3.
\end{aligned}
\] Write \(A\), \(x\), and \(b\). Square / over / under?
W2. Span interpretation. Let \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\2&4\end{bmatrix},\quad
b=\begin{bmatrix}3\\6\end{bmatrix},\quad
c=\begin{bmatrix}3\\5\end{bmatrix}.
\] (a) Are the columns of \(A\) independent? Describe \(\operatorname{span}\{\text{columns}\}\). (b) Does \(Ax=b\) have a solution? Infinitely many? (c) Does \(Ax=c\) have a solution?
W3. Context → \(Ax=b\). A café sells tea (\(\$2\)) and coffee (\(\$3\)). On Monday they sold \(x_1\) teas and \(x_2\) coffees for \(\$26\) total revenue, and sold \(10\) drinks in all. Write the two equations and the matrix form. Square?
W4. Anticipating outcomes. Without fully solving, say what you expect (and why) for:

\(2\) equations, \(2\) unknowns, with clearly parallel incompatible lines.
\(1\) equation, \(3\) unknowns: \(x_1+x_2+x_3=5\).
\(3\) equations, \(2\) unknowns that happen to be consistent (e.g. the third is the sum of the first two).

title: Lecture 21 — Systems and \(Ax=b\)
text:
Your turn
Y1. Write as \(Ax=b\): \[
\begin{aligned}
3x_1 - x_2 &= 0 \\
x_1 + 4x_2 &= 7.
\end{aligned}
\] Classify as square / over / under.
Y2. Let \(A\) have columns \(a_1=(1,0,1)\) and \(a_2=(0,1,1)\). For \(b=(1,1,2)\), explain in one sentence why \(Ax=b\) has a solution, and give one solution \(x\).
Y3. True or false, with a one-line reason: every square system \(Ax=b\) has exactly one solution.
Y4. A sensor gives \(4\) linear measurements for \(2\) unknown parameters. Is the system typically overdetermined? Does that guarantee inconsistency?






NoteAnswers (Your turn only)





Y1. \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}3&-1\\1&4\end{bmatrix},\quad
x=\begin{bmatrix}x_1\\x_2\end{bmatrix},\quad
b=\begin{bmatrix}0\\7\end{bmatrix}.
\] Square (\(m=n=2\)).
Y2. \(b=1\cdot a_1+1\cdot a_2\), so \(b\) is in the column span; one solution is \(x=(1,1)\).
Y3. False. Square systems can be inconsistent (parallel lines) or have infinitely many solutions (same line twice).
Y4. Typically overdetermined (\(m=4>n=2\)). No — consistency depends on whether \(b\) lands in a \(2\)-dimensional column space; it might or might not.

title: Lecture 22 — Gaussian elimination
text:
Learning objectives
By the end of class, you should be able to:

Perform elementary row operations.
Reduce a small augmented matrix to echelon form.
Solve a small system using back substitution.
Explain why row operations preserve the solution set.

title: Lecture 22 — Gaussian elimination
text:
Warm-up
For the system \[
\begin{aligned}
x_1 + 2x_2 &= 5 \\
2x_1 + 3x_2 &= 8,
\end{aligned}
\] write the augmented matrix \([A\mid b]\). What does each row mean as an equation?

title: Lecture 22 — Gaussian elimination
text:
Fill in
The augmented matrix of \(Ax=b\) is the matrix \([A\mid b]\) with \(A\) on the left and \(b\) as an extra \(\underline{\hspace{1.4cm}}\).
Elementary row operations (EROs) that do not change the solution set:

\(\underline{\hspace{3.6cm}}\) two rows.
Multiply a row by a \(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\) scalar.
Add a \(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\) of one row to another row.

Why they preserve solutions: each ERO is reversible (undo with another ERO), so the new system is \(\underline{\hspace{2.4cm}}\) to the old one — same solution set.
Gaussian elimination aims for (row) echelon form: zeros \(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\) each pivot, pivots marching right as you go down. Then back substitution solves from the \(\underline{\hspace{1.6cm}}\) equation upward.

title: Lecture 22 — Gaussian elimination
text:
Worked in class
W1. One ERO. Starting from \[
\begin{bmatrix}
1 & 2 & | & 5 \\
2 & 3 & | & 8
\end{bmatrix},
\] replace Row 2 by (Row 2) \(-\) \(2\cdot\)(Row 1). Write the new matrix and the matching equation for the new Row 2.
W2. Finish and back-substitute. Continue W1 to echelon form, then solve for \(x_2\) and \(x_1\).
W3. A \(3\times 3\) warm-up. Reduce \[
\begin{bmatrix}
1 & 1 & 1 & | & 6 \\
0 & 1 & 2 & | & 5 \\
2 & 1 & 0 & | & 5
\end{bmatrix}
\] to echelon form (you choose the EROs). Do not fully RREF unless time; stop when back substitution is clear. Solve.
W4. Why not “just swap randomly”? Explain in one sentence why multiplying a row by \(0\) is not an allowed ERO for solving systems.

title: Lecture 22 — Gaussian elimination
text:
Your turn
Y1. Augmented matrix for \[
\begin{aligned}
x_1 - x_2 &= 1 \\
3x_1 + 2x_2 &= 12.
\end{aligned}
\]
Y2. Perform one elimination step: clear the \((2,1)\) entry of \[
\begin{bmatrix}
1 & -1 & | & 1 \\
3 & 2 & | & 12
\end{bmatrix}
\] by a row replacement. Write the new matrix.
Y3. From the echelon form \[
\begin{bmatrix}
1 & -1 & | & 1 \\
0 & 5 & | & 9
\end{bmatrix},
\] solve by back substitution.
Y4. True or false, with a one-line reason: if you swap two rows of \([A\mid b]\), the solution set of \(Ax=b\) can change.






NoteAnswers (Your turn only)





Y1. \[
\begin{bmatrix}
1 & -1 & | & 1 \\
3 & 2 & | & 12
\end{bmatrix}.
\]
Y2. Row2 \(\leftarrow\) Row2 \(-\) \(3\cdot\)Row1 gives \[
\begin{bmatrix}
1 & -1 & | & 1 \\
0 & 5 & | & 9
\end{bmatrix}.
\]
Y3. From Row 2: \(5x_2=9\) so \(x_2=9/5\). From Row 1: \(x_1-x_2=1\) so \(x_1=1+9/5=14/5\). Solution \(x=(14/5,\,9/5)\).
Y4. False. Swapping rows is an elementary row operation; it reorders equations but keeps the same solution set.

title: Lecture 23 — RREF, pivots, free variables, and software
text:
Learning objectives
By the end of class, you should be able to:

Interpret reduced row echelon form.
Identify pivot and free variables.
Describe a solution set parametrically.
Distinguish inconsistent, unique, and infinite-solution cases.
Use software to solve or row-reduce a system and verify the answer using a residual.

title: Lecture 23 — RREF, pivots, free variables, and software
text:
Warm-up
The RREF of an augmented matrix is \[
\begin{bmatrix}
1 & 0 & 2 & | & 3 \\
0 & 1 & -1 & | & 4 \\
0 & 0 & 0 & | & 0
\end{bmatrix}.
\] Which variables are pivots? Which are free? Write the general solution.

title: Lecture 23 — RREF, pivots, free variables, and software
text:
Fill in
Reduced row echelon form (RREF) is echelon form with these extras:

Each pivot is \(\underline{\hspace{0.8cm}}\).
Each pivot is the \(\underline{\hspace{1.6cm}}\) nonzero in its column (zeros above and below).

A pivot variable (basic variable) corresponds to a pivot column. A free variable has \(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\) pivot in its column; assign a parameter (e.g. \(x_3=t\)).
Reading the RREF of \([A\mid b]\):







Pattern
Conclusion




A row \([0\ \cdots\ 0\mid c]\) with \(c\neq 0\)
\(\underline{\hspace{2.4cm}}\)


Every column of \(A\) has a pivot, and consistent
\(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\) solution


Consistent, and at least one free variable
\(\underline{\hspace{2.4cm}}\) solutions



Software. Use a solver or RREF command (Octave rref, Python SymPy rref, or a course helper). Always verify a candidate \(x\) by computing the residual \(Ax-b\) (should be near \(\underline{\hspace{1.0cm}}\)).

title: Lecture 23 — RREF, pivots, free variables, and software
text:
Worked in class
W1. Classify from RREF (no original system needed).

\[
\begin{bmatrix}
1 & 0 & | & 2 \\
0 & 1 & | & -1
\end{bmatrix}
\]
\[
\begin{bmatrix}
1 & 2 & | & 3 \\
0 & 0 & | & 1
\end{bmatrix}
\]
\[
\begin{bmatrix}
1 & 2 & 0 & | & 1 \\
0 & 0 & 1 & | & 4
\end{bmatrix}
\]

W2. Parametric form. From \[
\begin{bmatrix}
1 & 3 & 0 & | & 2 \\
0 & 0 & 1 & | & -1
\end{bmatrix},
\] identify free variable(s) and write \(x=(x_1,x_2,x_3)\) in terms of parameter(s).
W3. Software + residual. For \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\3&4\end{bmatrix},\quad
b=\begin{bmatrix}5\\11\end{bmatrix},
\] solve \(Ax=b\) with Octave or Python. Compute \(Ax-b\) and confirm it is (numerically) zero.
Octave sketch: A\[b] or rref([A b]) then read \(x\).
Python sketch: np.linalg.solve(A,b) for square invertible \(A\), or SymPy Matrix.hstack(A,b).rref().
W4. Inconsistent check. Invent a \(2\times 2\) augmented RREF that is inconsistent. What would \(Ax-b\) look like if software “forced” a least-squares answer? (One sentence — foreshadow Week 15.)

title: Lecture 23 — RREF, pivots, free variables, and software
text:
Your turn
Y1. From RREF \[
\begin{bmatrix}
1 & 0 & -2 & | & 5 \\
0 & 1 & 3 & | & -1 \\
0 & 0 & 0 & | & 0
\end{bmatrix},
\] list pivot variables, free variables, and the general solution.
Y2. True or false: if RREF has a row of all zeros including the augmented entry, the system is inconsistent.
Y3. You solve \(Ax=b\) in software and get \(x=(1,-1)\). You compute \(Ax-b=(0.0,\,10^{-15})\). Was the solve successful? Why check the residual?
Y4. A \(3\times 5\) matrix \(A\) (after RREF of \([A\mid b]\), consistent) has \(3\) pivots. How many free variables? Unique solution or infinitely many?

title: Lecture 23 — RREF, pivots, free variables, and software
text:
Lab 1, same day
After the short lecture: Lab 1 — Finding Similar Things. Distances, nearest neighbor, and a scale warning. Preview the one-pager; write on the hard copy in class.






NoteAnswers (Your turn only)





Y1. Pivot variables \(x_1,x_2\); free \(x_3=t\). Then \(x_1-2t=5\) and \(x_2+3t=-1\), so \[
x=(5+2t,\,-1-3t,\,t),\quad t\in\mathbb{R}.
\]
Y2. False. A zero row including the right-hand side is consistent (redundant equation). Inconsistency needs \([0\ \cdots\ 0\mid c]\) with \(c\neq 0\).
Y3. Yes — residual is numerically zero (roundoff). Checking \(Ax-b\) catches wrong \(x\), singular/ill-conditioned cases, and copy-paste mistakes.
Y4. \(n=5\) unknowns and \(3\) pivots \(\Rightarrow\) \(2\) free variables \(\Rightarrow\) infinitely many solutions (when consistent).

title: Lecture 24 — Linear dynamical systems
text:
Learning objectives
By the end of class, you should be able to:

Represent an evolving system as \(x_{t+1}=Ax_t\).
Interpret the state vector and transition matrix.
Build a transition matrix from a flow description.
Compute and interpret the next few states.

title: Lecture 24 — Linear dynamical systems
text:
Warm-up
From Lecture 19, the matrix \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}0.9&0.2\\ 0.1&0.8\end{bmatrix}
\] sends (urban, rural) population fractions today to tomorrow. If today’s state is \(x_0=(0.6,0.4)\), compute \(x_1=Ax_0\). In one sentence: what do the two entries of \(x_1\) mean?

title: Lecture 24 — Linear dynamical systems
text:
Fill in
A linear dynamical system (discrete time) has the form \[
x_{t+1}=\underline{\hspace{1.6cm}},
\] where \(t=0,1,2,\ldots\) is the time index.

The state \(x_t\) is an \(n\)-vector that completely describes the system at time \(t\).
The matrix \(A\) is the dynamics / transition matrix. Its size is \(\underline{\hspace{1.6cm}}\) (same \(n\) as the state).

Interpretation of columns. The \(j\)th column of \(A\) is the next state if the current state is \(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\) (one unit in compartment \(j\), nothing elsewhere).
A few steps by hand. \[
x_1=Ax_0,\qquad x_2=Ax_1=A(Ax_0),\qquad x_3=Ax_2=\cdots.
\] (We will package “\(t\) steps at once” as \(A^t\) later; today focus on one step at a time.)
Building \(A\) from a flow story. For each compartment \(j\), ask: if everything starts in \(j\), where does it go next? Those destinations become column \(j\).

title: Lecture 24 — Linear dynamical systems
text:
Worked in class
W1. State and matrix. A campus tracks (on-campus residents, off-campus) each week as a \(2\)-vector \(x_t\). Someone proposes \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}0.7&0.15\\ 0.3&0.85\end{bmatrix}.
\] (a) What does entry \(A_{12}\) mean in words? (b) What does the first column of \(A\) represent? (c) If \(x_0=(800,200)\), compute \(x_1\) and interpret both entries (people, not fractions).
W2. Build \(A\) from flows. Two towns, Arcata and Eureka, exchange residents each year:

Of those in Arcata, \(80\%\) stay and \(20\%\) move to Eureka.
Of those in Eureka, \(90\%\) stay and \(10\%\) move to Arcata.

Order the state as \(x_t=(\text{Arcata},\text{Eureka})\). Write the \(2\times 2\) transition matrix \(A\).
W3. Next few states. With \(A\) from W2 and \(x_0=(5000,7000)\), compute \(x_1\) and \(x_2\) by hand. Does the Arcata population rise or fall over these two years?
W4. Epidemic sketch (Boyd-style). Let \(x_t=(S_t,I_t)\) be (susceptible, infected) counts among a fixed population of size \(N=S_t+I_t\). A simple model uses \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}0.95&0.10\\ 0.05&0.90\end{bmatrix}.
\] (a) Check that each column sums to \(1\). Why is that natural here? (b) If \(x_0=(190,10)\), compute \(x_1\). Did infections go up or down?

title: Lecture 24 — Linear dynamical systems
text:
Your turn
Y1. True or false, with a one-line reason: if \(x_{t+1}=Ax_t\), then knowing \(x_t\) and \(A\) determines \(x_{t+1}\) uniquely.
Y2. Three age groups (youth, adult, senior) with transition \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}
0.6 & 0 & 0 \\
0.4 & 0.7 & 0 \\
0 & 0.3 & 0.8
\end{bmatrix}.
\] Interpret \(A_{21}\) and \(A_{33}\) in one phrase each. If \(x_0=(100,200,50)\), compute \(x_1\).
Y3. Build \(A\). Two warehouse inventory levels \(x_t=(\text{A},\text{B})\). Each day:

Warehouse A keeps \(70\%\) of its stock and ships \(30\%\) to B.
Warehouse B keeps \(60\%\) and ships \(40\%\) to A.

Write \(A\). Then with \(x_0=(100,50)\), find \(x_1\).
Y4. With \(A=\begin{bmatrix}1.1&0\\0&0.5\end{bmatrix}\) and \(x_0=(2,8)\), compute \(x_1\) and \(x_2\). Which component is growing? Which is shrinking?






NoteAnswers (Your turn only)





Y1. True. The rule \(x_{t+1}=Ax_t\) is a function of the current state: one matrix–vector product gives the unique next state.
Y2. \(A_{21}=0.4\): fraction (or count factor) of youth that become adults in one step. \(A_{33}=0.8\): fraction of seniors that remain seniors. \[
x_1=Ax_0=\begin{bmatrix}60\\180\\100\end{bmatrix}.
\]
Y3. \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}0.7&0.4\\ 0.3&0.6\end{bmatrix},\qquad
x_1=\begin{bmatrix}90\\60\end{bmatrix}.
\] (Column 1: keep \(70\%\) in A, ship \(30\%\) to B. Column 2: ship \(40\%\) of B to A, keep \(60\%\) in B.)
Y4. \(x_1=(2.2,4)\), \(x_2=(2.42,2)\). First component grows (factor \(1.1\) each step); second shrinks (factor \(0.5\)).

title: Lecture 25 — Simulation and long-run behavior
text:
Learning objectives
By the end of class, you should be able to:

Simulate many time steps computationally.
Plot state components through time.
Recognize stabilization, growth, decay, or oscillation.
Conduct a simple what-if simulation.
State limitations of a linear dynamical model.

title: Lecture 25 — Simulation and long-run behavior
text:
Warm-up
With \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}0.8&0.3\\ 0.2&0.7\end{bmatrix},\qquad x_0=\begin{bmatrix}1\\0\end{bmatrix},
\] compute \(x_1\) and \(x_2\) by hand. Guess (no calculator marathon): after many steps, will \(x_t\) blow up, shrink to zero, or settle somewhere nonzero?

title: Lecture 25 — Simulation and long-run behavior
text:
Fill in
Simulation recipe (any language):

Choose \(A\) and initial state \(x_0\).
For \(t=0,1,\ldots,T-1\): set \(x_{t+1}=\underline{\hspace{1.4cm}}\).
Store or plot the components of \(x_0,x_1,\ldots,x_T\) versus time.

Long-run patterns (names only — recognize from plots / tables):







Pattern
What you see




Stabilization
\(x_t\) approaches a fixed vector (or settles in magnitude)


Growth
components grow without bound (often roughly geometric)


Decay
components shrink toward \(\underline{\hspace{1.0cm}}\)


Oscillation
components bounce / cycle in sign or value



What-if. Change one thing — a parameter inside \(A\), or the initial state \(x_0\) — and re-simulate. Compare the two trajectories.
Limitations of \(x_{t+1}=Ax_t\). The model is \(\underline{\hspace{2.4cm}}\) (no \(x^2\) terms, no products of states); \(A\) is assumed constant; time is discrete; there is no noise, capacity limit, or policy change unless you build it into \(A\). Real systems may only match the model for a while.

title: Lecture 25 — Simulation and long-run behavior
text:
Worked in class
W1. Many steps on the board / laptop. Let \[

title: Lecture 27 — Matrix multiplication
text:
Warm-up
Let \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\0&-1\end{bmatrix},\qquad
B=\begin{bmatrix}0&1\\3&2\end{bmatrix},\qquad
x=\begin{bmatrix}1\\-1\end{bmatrix}.
\]

What are the dimensions of \(A\) and of \(B\)? Is \(AB\) defined? If so, what size is it?
Compute \(Bx\) (a \(2\)-vector). You will need this later as “\(B\) first, then \(A\).”

title: Lecture 27 — Matrix multiplication
text:
Fill in
If \(A\) is \(m\times n\) and \(B\) is \(n\times p\), the product \(AB\) is the \(m\times p\) matrix whose \(j\)th column is \[
(AB)_j = \underline{\hspace{2.4cm}}.
\] Equivalently, entry \((i,j)\) is the inner product of \(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\) of \(A\) with \(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\) of \(B\): \[
(AB)_{ij} = a_i^{\mathsf{T}} b_j.
\]
When is \(AB\) defined? The inner dimensions must match: number of \(\underline{\hspace{1.6cm}}\) of \(A\) equals number of \(\underline{\hspace{1.6cm}}\) of \(B\).
Associativity (for vectors). For a compatible \(p\)-vector \(x\), \[
(AB)x = A(Bx).
\] Reading right to left: apply \(\underline{\hspace{1.0cm}}\) first, then \(\underline{\hspace{1.0cm}}\). So \(ABx\) is a sequence of transformations.
Not commutative. In general \(AB\neq BA\) (even when both products are defined). Order of maps matters: “rotate then reflect” is not the same as “reflect then rotate.”

title: Lecture 27 — Matrix multiplication
text:
Worked in class
W1. Dimensions. For each pair, decide whether \(AB\) is defined and give the size of \(AB\) if it is.

\(A\) is \(3\times 2\), \(B\) is \(2\times 4\).
\(A\) is \(2\times 3\), \(B\) is \(2\times 4\).
\(A\) is \(2\times 2\), \(B\) is \(2\times 2\).

W2. Compute a product. With \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\0&-1\end{bmatrix},\qquad
B=\begin{bmatrix}0&1\\3&2\end{bmatrix},
\] compute \(AB\) by forming columns \(Ab_1\) and \(Ab_2\) (or by row–column inner products).
W3. Sequence of maps. Using the same \(A\), \(B\), and \(x=(1,-1)\) from the warm-up, compute \(Bx\), then \(A(Bx)\). Compare with \((AB)x\) using your \(AB\) from W2. Same answer?
W4. Non-commutativity. With the same \(A\) and \(B\), compute \(BA\). Is \(BA=AB\)?

title: Lecture 27 — Matrix multiplication
text:
Your turn
Y1. Let \[
C=\begin{bmatrix}1&0&-1\\2&1&0\end{bmatrix},\qquad
D=\begin{bmatrix}0&1\\1&0\\2&-1\end{bmatrix}.
\] Is \(CD\) defined? Size? Compute \(CD\).
Y2. Is \(DC\) defined? If so, give its size (you need not compute every entry unless time allows). What does this say about “\(CD\) vs \(DC\)”?
Y3. Let \(R=\begin{bmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{bmatrix}\) (\(90^\circ\) CCW) and \(S=\operatorname{diag}(2,1)\) (horizontal stretch). Compute \(RSx\) and \(SRx\) for \(x=(1,0)\). Same point? Interpret in one sentence.
Y4. True or false, with a one-line reason: if \(AB\) and \(BA\) are both defined, then \(A\) and \(B\) must be square of the same size.






NoteAnswers (Your turn only)





Y1. \(C\) is \(2\times 3\), \(D\) is \(3\times 2\), so \(CD\) is defined and \(2\times 2\): \[
CD=\begin{bmatrix}-2&2\\1&2\end{bmatrix}.
\] (Columns: \(Cd_1=(-2,1)\), \(Cd_2=(2,2)\).)
Y2. Yes — \(D\) is \(3\times 2\) and \(C\) is \(2\times 3\), so \(DC\) is \(3\times 3\). Even when both products exist they need not have the same size, so they cannot be equal as matrices. Order matters.
Y3. \(Sx=(2,0)\), then \(RSx=(0,2)\). Meanwhile \(Rx=(0,1)\), then \(SRx=(0,1)\). Different: stretch-then-rotate \(\neq\) rotate-then-stretch for this \(x\).
Y4. False. Example: \(A\) is \(2\times 3\) and \(B\) is \(3\times 2\) — both \(AB\) (\(2\times 2\)) and \(BA\) (\(3\times 3\)) are defined, but neither factor is square. (They become the same size only when \(m=n\).)

title: Lecture 28 — Composition and matrix powers
Lecture 28 — Composition and matrix powers
text:
Fill in
Composition. If \(g(x)=Bx\) and \(f(y)=Ay\) (compatible sizes), then \[
(f\circ g)(x) = f(g(x)) = \underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}.
\] The matrix of the composed map is the \(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\) \(AB\) (apply \(B\) first). Multistage processes: write each stage as a matrix, then multiply in the right order.
Matrix powers. If \(A\) is square \(n\times n\), define \(A^0=I\), \(A^1=A\), and \[
A^{k} = \underline{\hspace{2.8cm}}
\] (\(k\) factors). Then \(A^{k+\ell}=A^k A^\ell\).
Dynamics connection. For \(x_{t+1}=Ax_t\) (Lab 4 / Lectures 24–26), \[
x_k = \underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}.
\] So iterating the recurrence \(k\) times is the same as one matrix–vector product with \(A^k\). Powers package “\(k\) steps of the system” into a single matrix.
Networks / paths. If \(A\) is an adjacency matrix (Boyd: \(A_{ij}=1\) means an edge from \(j\) to \(i\)), then \((A^k)_{ij}\) counts \(\underline{\hspace{3.6cm}}\) of length \(k\) from \(j\) to \(i\). Transition / population models: powers accumulate multi-step flow.

title: Lecture 28 — Composition and matrix powers
text:
Worked in class
W1. Multistage product. A population moves in two stages each year: migration \(B=\begin{bmatrix}0.8&0.1\\0.2&0.9\end{bmatrix}\), then growth/decay \(A=\operatorname{diag}(1.05,0.95)\). Write the one-year matrix \(M\) and compute \(M\begin{bmatrix}100\\100\end{bmatrix}\).
W2. Dynamics as a power. Let \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}0.5&0.5\\0&1\end{bmatrix},\qquad x_0=\begin{bmatrix}1\\0\end{bmatrix}.
\] Compute \(x_1=Ax_0\), \(x_2=Ax_1\), and \(A^2\). Check that \(x_2=A^2 x_0\).
W3. Entry interpretation. Directed graph on nodes \(\{1,2,3\}\) with edges \(1\to 2\), \(2\to 3\), \(3\to 1\), and also \(1\to 3\). Adjacency (Boyd convention): \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}
0 & 0 & 1 \\
1 & 0 & 0 \\
1 & 1 & 0
\end{bmatrix}.
\] Compute \(A^2\). What does \((A^2)_{31}\) mean? How many length-\(2\) walks from \(1\) to \(3\)?
W4. Why powers matter for Lab 4. In one sentence: if you already computed \(A^{10}\), how do you get \(x_{10}\) from \(x_0\) without looping ten times by hand?

title: Lecture 28 — Composition and matrix powers
text:
Your turn
Y1. Stage 1: \(B=\operatorname{diag}(2,1)\). Stage 2: \(A=\begin{bmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{bmatrix}\). Find \(M\) for “\(B\) then \(A\)” and compute \(M(1,1)\).
Y2. With \(A=\begin{bmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{bmatrix}\) (swap coordinates) and \(x_0=(3,1)\), compute \(A^2\) and \(x_2=A^2 x_0\). Interpret \(A^2\).
Y3. Using the adjacency matrix \(A\) from W3, compute \((A^2)_{22}\). Interpret: walks of length \(2\) that start and end at node \(2\).
Y4. True or false: for the dynamics \(x_{t+1}=Ax_t\), we always have \(x_{5}=A x_{4}\) and also \(x_{5}=A^{5}x_{0}\).






NoteAnswers (Your turn only)





Y1. \(M=AB=\begin{bmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2&0\\0&1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}0&-1\\2&0\end{bmatrix}\). Then \(M(1,1)=(-1,2)\).
Y2. \(A^2=I\) (swap twice returns to the start). \(x_2=A^2 x_0=(3,1)=x_0\). So \(A^2\) is the identity map — two swaps undo each other.
Y3. From W3, \[
A^2=\begin{bmatrix}
1 & 1 & 0 \\
0 & 0 & 1 \\
1 & 0 & 1
\end{bmatrix},
\] so \((A^2)_{22}=0\): there is no walk of length \(2\) from \(2\) back to \(2\). (From \(2\) the only edge is \(2\to 3\); from \(3\) you go to \(1\), not back to \(2\) in one more step.)
Y4. True. Both follow from \(x_{t+1}=Ax_t\) by induction: one step from \(x_4\), and five steps packaged as \(A^5\).

title: Lecture 29 — Same mathematics, very different computational cost
text:
Learning objectives
By the end of class, you should be able to:
